Every Monday, FerrumLine sends you the construction projects that changed in your trade and your territory, each one with the reason it is on your list.

  • The reading is done for you. Every week we read the records, filter them to your trades and territory, and write up what changed, with a reason on every line.

How business phones work

Every report now prints the business phone each named contractor filed with the CCB, matched by exact company name. Companies only. No homeowner or personal numbers, ever. When there is no exact match, no phone prints rather than a guess.

What a status badge means

A badge describes the records we found. It does not establish whether work is available, whether a contractor has been selected, or whether a project is ready to start.

For this sample, the available Portland mechanical-permit data runs through October 11, 2026. Later filings may not appear.

Every edition states its record cutoff date. Confirm the details against the official record before you act.

What went into this report: records read from 19 public feeds, city, county, state, and federal. 112,657 records on file (October 2026). Six record sets cross-matched against each other. Every row dated.

Built narrow, on purpose.

We cover three trades in two counties, and we go deep instead of wide. A report that covers everything tells you nothing first.

The report comes by email and stays private. There is no dashboard to log into and no list of subscribers anywhere. What you know on Monday morning is yours.

We read the public record so you don't have to. Records from city, county, state, and federal offices, cross-matched and tracked across about 140 facts per project, so the short list you get on Monday is the right list.

Why we built FerrumLine

Running a shop leaves little time to work through permit portals and planning files.

We bring relevant records together and explain what changed. Less digging, with the judgment left to you.

How we read a project

Most lists show you one record and stop. We read across records and say what each one supports.

A project history, built from records

A single permit filing is one data point. We connect the records that name the same project: the planning filing, the building permit, the trade permits that follow, the company names recorded on each. Each step keeps its date and a reference to the record behind it, so the history reads as a timeline you can follow.

Relevance, explained per trade

Every entry carries a one-line reason it is on your list, written for your trade. A mixed-use building with a mechanical permit already filed is flagged so you do not chase it. A new building with no trade permit on record is flagged as early. The reason is tied to the record it comes from.

What changed

Each week we report two things: newly found projects, and changes to projects we are already tracking. A status that moved, a company newly named, a filing that appeared since the last list. You see the movement, not just the roster.

Companies and roles, as recorded

Company names appear exactly as the record writes them. We do not assign roles the record does not give. A company named on a permit is reported as named on that permit, nothing more.

Documented bids stay separate from private work

Public solicitations are a documented record: a posting, a due date, an award. We keep those in their own stream, apart from private permit records. We never treat a phase label on a private permit as an open bid, and we never read a missing record as available work.

Evidence, dates, limits, next step

Every entry carries what we know and what we do not. The record, the date we checked it, and the limit of what it proves. Where the next move is yours, we say so: confirm the status, and read the official posting before you act.

2. Planning report for analysts

Spend your time on the analysis

A separate weekly planning report for development and research professionals.

We bring selected project records together so you can review the proposal, follow its recorded progress, and see what is still unknown.

A limited pilot with agreed scope

Before enrollment, we discuss the geography, project types, and recurring research tasks that matter to your work.

We then agree on what the pilot will include. We do not promise every market, every project, or every kind of analysis.

What the pilot can include

  • A watchlist of selected planning projects.
  • Recorded stages and filing dates.
  • Changes found between editions.
  • Applicant and project information from public records.
  • Zoning context from the city's published map, shown only where it checks out — anything uncertain is left out.

Zoning notes, not development verdicts

Where included, zoning notes separate documented facts, interpretation, and unknowns.

A proposed height or floor area may be compared with a sourced base-zone standard. Overlays, bonuses, exceptions, and other requirements can change what applies.

These notes are a starting point for further review, not a determination of what can be built.

How we will assess the pilot

We want to learn whether the report reduces collection work, makes project changes easier to follow, or brings useful records into your existing workflow.

Those are questions to test with you, not outcomes we assume.

Construction Momentum Score

IN DEVELOPMENT

A score we are building for the analyst report. It reads four things from the permit record: how many permits were filed this month compared with the three-month average; whether average permit values are rising or falling; how much of the work is new construction versus renovation; and how many permits were filed per 1,000 properties.

Scores are read against published home value context for the same area. When an area you follow moves sharply, we flag it in your Monday report and in a weekly market digest.

Built for analysts and investors who track where building is heating up. Part of the analyst report as it develops.

4. Commercial openings report

For commercial insurance producers

A weekly report of businesses that just received a permit or a license.

That filing is often the moment the business needs insurance. It can also be the moment the business changes the insurance it has.

The report puts that moment in front of you while it is still new.

What shows up in the report

  • A restaurant or bar with a new liquor license.
  • A business opening a new location, with a building permit or a new business filing.
  • A company formed this week, in the state business filings.
  • A new trucking company that cannot start work yet. The next block says why.

New trucking companies

A new trucking company needs federal operating authority before it can work. The authority stays pending until the company's insurance is filed with the federal motor carrier office (FMCSA).

The report lists new carriers in your territory whose authority is still pending. Each one needs insurance before it can run. That is the opening.

What one row shows

  • The business name, as the record writes it.
  • What was filed: a permit, a license, a new business filing, or trucking authority.
  • The date it was filed.
  • The address or county on the record.
  • The stage: filed, issued, or still pending.
  • A reference to the official record, so you can check it yourself.
  • A business phone only when a public record prints one. Personal phone numbers never print.

Every report prints the date its records are current through. If nothing changed in your territory that week, the report prints one line saying so.

What works now, and what is planned

We draw a hard line between what the product does today and what is still being built. What follows is everything on each side.

What works now

  • Clark County, Washington weekly issued-permits reporting, read as the county writes it. Where the county report does not name a contractor, we print that plainly instead of guessing. We keep the county's calculated valuation and the applicant's estimated value in separate columns, and neither is presented as a project budget.
  • Honest badges on every entry. Example: "Electrical permit filed by [company] on [date]."
  • A reference to the official record on every entry, with the date the record was checked.
  • Every entry states what is documented and what remains unknown, in plain words.
  • A missing permit never proves work is available. A named contractor on an issued permit changes how we read the record; it does not delete the entry.

Planned, not yet in the product

Each item below is planned, not yet in the product. None of it is available now, and none of it is promised with enrollment.

  • Construction Momentum Score. In development. First test scores were computed for September 2026 and are being checked before any are published.
  • Permit-detail refresh before delivery. Planned, not yet in the product. We would re-check each permit's status, issue date, named companies, and scope notes before a report ships, so stale findings like "not yet filed" get retired.
  • Scope-text parsing on permit records. Planned, not yet in the product. We would preserve the record's raw scope wording and flag wordings such as "No Construction On This Permit," without reading separate-permit notes as open work.
  • Licensing reference lines on trade entries. Planned, not yet in the product. A one-line jurisdiction note of general licensing information on electrical and plumbing entries. These notes would never be presented as a check of a named company's standing.
  • Parcel and site matching. Planned, not yet in the product. Matching records to the same site using authoritative site identifiers, keeping raw and normalized addresses separate, and stating the issuing jurisdiction apart from the postal city.
  • Planning-to-permit joins. Planned, not yet in the product. Connecting dated planning and land-use records to later permits as context where the records support it. A proposal is not an approval, a funding, a permit, or an award.
  • Licensing credential checks. Planned, not yet in the product. Checking the actual license standing of named companies, with the date each one was checked. Until then, license standing is stated as unchecked.
  • Procurement solicitation stream. Planned, not yet in the product. A separate watchlist of documented public solicitations, deadlines, addenda, and awards, kept in its own stream and never forced onto private permit records.
  • Capital-improvement watchlist. Planned, not yet in the product. A separate procurement-stage watchlist for public projects, with new and changed entries, trade fit, solicitation references, and permit overlap tracked weekly.
  • Business-context enrichment. Planned, not yet in the product. Bounded address-level background, such as occupancy history or lease marketing, recorded with source, time spent, and whether it changed any decision.

Clark County commercial reuse of bulk permit data is still under legal review. Our coverage descriptions will not promise what that review has not cleared.

Coverage and freshness

Portland, Oregon and Clark County, Washington. Contractor, analyst, and tree reports all draw from records in these two areas. We do not cover statewide or national data.

  • Portland trade-permit records are current through October 11, 2026. This covers mechanical (HVAC), electrical, and plumbing. Mechanical filed-status matching is also current through October 11. The intake records behind these permits have not been updated since that date.
  • Clark County, Washington records come from the county's weekly issued-permits report, for the reporting period October 4 through October 11, 2026. Our bulk public-records request to the county is pending; the county's response is due October 23.

When the records start moving again, we update the cutoff date on this page.

Two things we say plainly:

  • Trade permits carry no dollar values. Where the record carries a value, we print it as written and label its type: the county's calculated valuation and the applicant's estimated value are kept apart, and neither is presented as a project budget.
  • Clark County's weekly report does not name contractors. Where no contractor is named, the entry says so instead of guessing.

Every entry names the issuing agency. We keep the issuing jurisdiction separate from the postal city, because they are not always the same.

No. The contractor report describes projects found in public records.

A filing does not mean the owner has requested quotes or that subcontractor selection remains open.

Does a missing mechanical permit mean work is available?

No. It means we did not find a matching record in the available data through the stated cutoff.

A contractor may already be selected, a later permit may exist, or the matching process may not capture it.

Does a filed permit mean I should ignore a project?

Not necessarily. It tells you that a matching filing appears in the reviewed records.

Whether the project is relevant to your business requires further checking.

How current is the information?

Each edition states its record dates and known gaps.

A newly generated report can still contain information from records that have stopped updating. We make that distinction clear.

Do you include homeowner contact information?

No homeowner names, personal phone numbers, or personal contact details are included in the reports.

Business names appear when the public record includes them.

Does anyone else receive the same report?

On the contractor report, no second shop gets your trade's list in your county.

One shop holds each trade in each county. That shop is the only one that gets that trade's list for that county while it subscribes. When it stops, the seat opens.

For the other reports, we confirm the scope of your report before enrollment.

Can I request different coverage?

Yes. Tell us what you need.

A request helps us understand demand. It does not mean that coverage is currently available.

How do I cancel?

Reply to any report email and say cancel, or call or text us.

Cancelling stops the next renewal. The report keeps coming through the date you have paid for. There is no lock-in period.

What if I find an error?

Send us the project or notice, the issue you found, and a source if you have one.

We will review it and correct the report where needed.

Subscription policies

Draft for review

The plain version of what a subscription means. Items marked as draft defaults are our standard small-business starting point, and each one still needs John's final sign-off.

Settled

  • Opt-in only. Paid service starts only when you subscribe through Stripe checkout and enter your own payment details. We never convert a sample or preview to paid service on our own, and no subscription starts until you complete checkout yourself.
  • Cancellation. Cancel anytime by replying to a report email, or by phone or text. Cancellation stops the next renewal.
  • Paid-through service. Service runs through your paid-through date. What is paid for is delivered, even after you cancel.
  • Term. Month to month. There is no lock-in period and no long-term contract.
  • Price. $79 a month per selected report, pilot pricing. No setup fee. One contractor report covering all three trades is $79 a month, not $237.

Draft defaults, pending John's sign-off

Each of these is written as a standard starting point. None is final until confirmed.

  • Taxes. Sales tax, if required in your jurisdiction, is added to the $79 monthly charge and shown as a separate line on your receipt. (draft default — John to confirm or change)
  • Billing date. Your card is charged on the same calendar date each month, starting the day paid service begins. If that date does not exist in a month (for example, the 31st), the charge runs on the last day of the month. (draft default — John to confirm or change)
  • Failed delivery. If we cannot deliver a weekly report to the email you gave us, we retry for three business days and then contact you at the phone number on file to confirm your address. A report we could not deliver is not lost; we resend it to your corrected address. (draft default — John to confirm or change)
  • Price-change notice. If the pilot price changes, we tell you by email at least 30 days before the change takes effect. The new price applies only to renewals after the notice period. (draft default — John to confirm or change)
  • Refunds. If you cancel mid-month, the current month is not refunded; service runs through your paid-through date. (draft default — John to confirm or change)

What the list cannot be used for

The list is project information from public records. It cannot be used for credit, insurance, employment, or housing decisions about any person. FerrumLine is not a consumer reporting agency.

Public records have errors and lag. We check every list before it goes out, but we cannot promise every entry is current or correct. Always confirm a project on the public record before you act on it.

How you contact anyone is your responsibility. You are expected to follow telemarketing and texting laws.

Why I started FerrumLine

I'm John Linneman.

I started in hardwood flooring, doing the groundwork that comes before the finished floor. Later, selling IT to hospitals taught me how much research and timing matter in a business relationship.

FerrumLine brings those interests together: understanding how projects progress and making the information easier to use.

I built this construction research and reporting service for people who need to follow the work but do not have hours to spend sorting through records.

It is still a pilot. The reports are being tested with people who work in the industries they cover.

Coverage and limitations

Where the information comes from

We monitor public bid boards and permit records across the covered region: Portland, Oregon, and Clark County, Washington. Depending on the report and the scope agreed with you, that can include permit and planning records, public bid postings from local, state, and federal agencies, and federal award records.

Customer reports include record-level references for the entries they contain. We do not publish the full list of boards and records we monitor.

What we do with the records

We collect relevant records, join related entries where possible, compare editions, and explain the findings in plain language.

Public records can contain errors, missing fields, inconsistent names, and delayed updates. Our matching and interpretation can also be incomplete or incorrect.

What the reports are for

The reports support project research and procurement monitoring.

They do not determine project funding, contractor availability, bidding eligibility, code compliance, or development feasibility. Check the official records and obtain appropriate professional advice where needed.

The reports are not intended for credit, insurance, employment, or housing decisions about individuals.

Pilot arrangements

Before enrollment, we provide the report scope, price, billing arrangements, cancellation process, and any trial or refund terms.

Those agreed terms govern the pilot. This page does not itself enroll you or authorize a charge.
